content:
Apple officially announced the Apple Upgrade leasing program today, and it works exactly as the outside world expected. Although the monthly fee makes the product more affordable, users may at any time fall into an endless cycle of leasing.

That said, the biggest difference between this program and the iPhone Upgrade Program it partially replaces is that you won't actually own the device after the contract ends...

Apple product pricing has never been this high, and the appeal of a monthly fee model making hardware more affordable is undeniable. Looking at the monthly payments alone, the Apple Upgrade program does indeed achieve this.

Take the MacBook Pro with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage as an example — the monthly rental starts as low as US$38.99. This approach makes it possible for more consumers to get their hands on Apple products, and that is undoubtedly a good thing.

The Hidden Worries of the Apple Upgrade Program

The problem is exactly as I predicted last week: people will approach this program with the same mindset as leasing a car. Although you can choose to pay off the remaining balance in one lump sum at the end of the lease and take the car away, in practice almost no one does that. Most car lessees simply return the old car and lease a new one, over and over again.

The Apple Upgrade program could easily end up in the same situation. If you want actual ownership of the device, you must pay off the difference between the total rental amount and the product's original price in one lump sum at the end of the term.

Here's an example using the MacBook Pro mentioned above (totals rounded to the nearest US dollar):

36-month plan

  • Monthly rental: US$38.99
  • Total paid over the term: US$1,403
  • Balloon payment to take ownership: US$585

24-month plan

  • Monthly rental: US$53.99
  • Total paid over the term: US$1,295
  • Balloon payment to take ownership: US$703

For someone who couldn't afford to buy the machine outright in the first place, this balloon payment is by no means small. Unless they've been setting aside the difference throughout the leasing period, it's very likely they won't be able to afford it. So the most probable outcome is simply starting another new cycle.

If You Can Afford It, the Smartest Move

If you can handle a slightly higher monthly payment, the smartest move is to take matters into your own hands and reshape the program into something equivalent to the original IUP.

You keep paying the monthly rental to Apple, while at the same time opening a separate savings account and setting aside a sum each month, ready to cover the balloon payment when the term ends. Using that 36-month MBP lease as an example, the numbers would look roughly like this:

  • Monthly rental: US$38.99
  • Monthly savings contribution: US$16.26
  • Total monthly outlay: US$55.25
  • Total paid to Apple: US$1,403
  • Amount saved toward the balloon payment: US$585.36 (before interest)

Top-liked comment from netizen Ryan Lounsbury

I'd probably use this leasing program to switch out my iPhone. I tend to upgrade every 12 to 24 months or so. So as long as there's no interest, I can basically keep using the latest model without having to put up the full purchase price all at once. Given my upgrade habits, this approach makes a lot of sense.

However, Apple has slipped a poison pill into its Upgrade/leasing program — to participate, you have to sign on with a designated carrier partner and activate network service. I've been using Mint Mobile for years; if I don't follow this rule, I can't lease the device, and I'd even have to pay a penalty — it's absolutely outrageous.

When the time comes, you can use the money you've saved to pay that US$585 balloon payment and officially take ownership of the device, making it completely yours.

Of course, if you really want to upgrade to a new device, selling off the old one you own and leasing a new one is completely fine too. The secondhand selling price is usually enough to offset the balloon payment on the new contract — just drop it into the savings account, and from then on your only monthly outlay is the rental fee.

How are you planning to fund your future Apple product purchases? Feel free to share in the comments.
